section.title: David Spares Saul Again
section.sectionRationale: For a second time the Ziphites betray David's location, and for a second time Saul comes hunting him with three thousand men, and for a second time David finds Saul utterly defenseless, this time asleep in the middle of his own camp. David slips in, takes the spear and water jug from beside Saul's head as proof, and again refuses to let Abishai strike the LORD's anointed. It is one movement: the settled conviction, tested twice now, that David must not seize the throne by violence but leave Saul's fate entirely to the LORD.
section.thesis: Given a second total opportunity to end his exile by killing Saul, David again refuses to lift his hand against the LORD's anointed, entrusting the timing and manner of Saul's downfall to God alone, a fixed resolve that marks him as a type of the greater King who would not grasp His kingdom by force.
section.frameNote: Five beats: Saul renews the hunt, verses 1 to 5; David and Abishai in the sleeping camp, verses 6 to 12; David's taunt across the ravine to Abner, verses 13 to 16; the exchange between David and Saul, verses 17 to 20; and Saul's confession and blessing, verses 21 to 25.

verses.text: Then the Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah and said, “Is not David hiding on the hill of Hachilah, opposite Jeshimon?”
So Saul, accompanied by three thousand chosen men of Israel, went down to the Wilderness of Ziph to search for David there.
Saul camped beside the road at the hill of Hachilah opposite Jeshimon, but David was living in the wilderness. When he realized that Saul had followed him there,
David sent out spies to verify that Saul had arrived.

Then David set out and went to the place where Saul had camped. He saw the place where Saul and Abner son of Ner, the general of his army, had lain down. Saul was lying inside the inner circle of the camp, with the troops camped around him.
David asked Ahimelech the Hittite and Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, “Who will go down with me to Saul in the camp?” “I will go with you,” answered Abishai.

That night David and Abishai came to the troops, and Saul was lying there asleep in the inner circle of the camp, with his spear stuck in the ground by his head. And Abner and the troops were lying around him.

Abishai said to David, “Today God has delivered your enemy into your hand. Now, therefore, please let me thrust the spear through him into the ground with one stroke. I will not need to strike him twice!”
But David said to Abishai, “Do not destroy him, for who can extend a {{yad|hand}} against the LORD’s {{mashiach|anointed}} and be guiltless?”
David added, “As surely as the LORD lives, the LORD Himself will strike him down; either his day will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and perish.
But the LORD forbid that I should extend my hand against the LORD’s anointed. Instead, take the spear and water jug by his head, and let us go.”

So David took the spear and water jug by Saul’s head, and they departed. No one saw them or knew about it, nor did anyone wake up; they all remained asleep, because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them.
Then David crossed to the other side and stood atop the mountain at a distance; there was a wide gulf between them.
And David shouted to the troops and to Abner son of Ner, “Will you not answer me, Abner?” “Who are you who calls to the king?” Abner replied.
So David said to Abner, “You are a man, aren’t you? And who in Israel is your equal? Why then did you not protect your lord the king when one of the people came to destroy him?

This thing you have done is not good. As surely as the LORD lives, all of you deserve to die, since you did not protect your lord, the LORD’s anointed. Now look around. Where are the king’s spear and water jug that were by his head?”

units.label: David appeals to Saul
units.note: what evil is in my hand

verses.text: Then Saul recognized David’s voice and asked, “Is that your voice, David my son?” “It is my voice, my lord and king,” David said.
And he continued, “Why is my lord pursuing his servant? What have I done? What evil is in my hand?

Now please, may my lord the king hear the words of his servant: If the LORD has stirred you up against me, then may He accept an offering. But if men have done it, may they be cursed in the presence of the LORD! For today they have driven me away from sharing in the inheritance of the LORD, saying, ‘Go, serve other gods.’
So do not let my blood fall to the ground far from the presence of the LORD. For the king of Israel has come out to look for a flea, like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains.”
Then Saul replied, “I have sinned. Come back, David my son. I will never harm you again, because today you considered my life precious. I have played the fool and have committed a grave error!”
“Here is the king’s spear,” David answered. “Let one of the young men come over and get it.

May the LORD repay every man for his {{tsedaqah|righteousness}} and faithfulness. For the LORD delivered you into my hand today, but I would not extend my hand against the LORD’s {{mashiach|anointed}}.
As surely as I valued your life today, so may the LORD value my life and rescue me from all trouble.”
Saul said to him, “May you be blessed, David my son. You will accomplish great things and will surely prevail.” So David went on his way, and Saul returned home.

mashiach.gloss: Anointed one. Saul was set apart for the throne by Samuel's anointing oil, and even though he hunts David without cause, David twice refuses to lift a hand against him for this reason alone, verses 9 and 23. The office belongs to the LORD's own choosing, not to whoever can seize it by the sword.

tsedaqah.gloss: Righteousness, right conduct, covenant faithfulness. David asks that the LORD Himself repay every man his tsedaqah, resting his reward on God's just character rather than on Saul's unstable gratitude, since Saul's own promises have already failed once before, in chapter 24.

yad.gloss: Hand, the seat of a person's power or action. Twice David refuses to extend his yad against the LORD's anointed, and he later asks Saul what evil is in his own hand, verse 18, framing the whole episode as a question of whose hand will act, and whose hand will be found innocent.

basic.context: This is the second time in as many episodes that David has Saul completely in his power. The Ziphites betray his location again, Saul comes hunting him with three thousand men, and David slips by night into the very heart of the sleeping camp, right beside Saul's head. His companion Abishai begs to end it with one thrust of the spear. But David refuses, a second time, to kill the man God anointed as king. Instead he takes the spear and water jug as evidence and shouts the proof across the valley at dawn, rebuking Abner for failing to guard the king. Confronted, Saul again confesses his sin and blesses David, though the two do not travel home together; David still will not trust his safety to Saul's word. The whole scene asks how an anointed but rejected king is meant to wait for God's kingdom rather than seize it for himself.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative describing David's own conviction about a specific king whom God had anointed; it is not a general command that every wrong must go unanswered or that lawful justice may never be pursued. What it does teach every reader is a settled trust that vindication and timing belong to the LORD, especially when we are wronged by those set in authority over us.
basic.originalLanguages: David will not raise a yad, hand, against the LORD's mashiach, anointed, even though Saul hunts him without cause. At the end he asks the LORD to repay every man his tsedaqah, righteousness, the very thing Saul's own word cannot reliably deliver.
basic.typology: David, God's anointed yet still uncrowned king, refuses again and again to seize the throne by violence, choosing instead to wait for God to act in His own time and way. This looks forward to great David's greater Son, who though truly King would not call down legions of angels or grasp an earthly throne by force, entrusting Himself instead to the Father's justice and timing.
basic.christ: David's refusal to strike the LORD's anointed, even when a companion urges it and the opportunity is total, anticipates the pattern fulfilled perfectly in Jesus Christ. Jesus, the true Anointed One, refused Peter's sword in Gethsemane and would not summon armies of angels to seize His kingdom by force, choosing instead the Father's path through suffering to glory. Like David, He entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly, and received His kingdom not by grasping but by humble obedience even to death, only then exalted by God Himself.
basic.god: God is shown as the true King over kings, the one who alone has the right to remove Saul in His own timing, whether by natural death or in battle. He casts a supernatural deep sleep over Saul's whole camp so David can act without bloodshed, and it is to Him that David appeals for vindication and reward rather than to human strength or opportunity. Even Saul, in a fleeting moment of honesty, recognizes that David's restraint flows from valuing what belongs to the LORD.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Samuel 24 records the first time David spares Saul, in the cave at En-gedi. 1 Peter 2 says Christ entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly. Matthew 26 shows Jesus refusing the sword in Gethsemane. Romans 12 says vengeance belongs to the LORD. Philippians 2 says Christ did not grasp at equality with God but humbled Himself.
basic.oneStory: David's second refusal to kill Saul is one more step in the long story of a king who will not seize his throne by violence, trusting the LORD's timing instead. It anticipates the true Anointed One, Jesus, who also refused to grasp His kingdom by force, and whose patient trust in the Father's justice becomes the pattern for all who suffer unjustly while awaiting God's vindication.

context.literary:
This chapter is best read as a controlled variation on chapter 24 rather than a simple repeat, and the differences are where the meaning sharpens. There David stumbles on Saul by chance, in a cave Saul enters to relieve himself; here David goes looking for Saul on purpose, sends spies to confirm the camp's location, verse 4, and walks in by design. There he only cuts a robe and is stricken with conscience even for that; here he takes an entire spear and water jug from beside a sleeping king's head and shows no second thoughts at all. The scene has moved from an accidental brush with temptation to a deliberate, planned test of the very same resolve, as though the narrator wants no reader to say the first refusal was a fluke of circumstance.

The chapter's four dialogues are arranged with mounting distance and mounting authority. Abishai speaks to David alone, in whispers, inside the sleeping camp, verses 8 to 11. David then shouts across a ravine to Abner, a rebuke aimed at a subordinate for failing his duty, verses 14 to 16. Only then does Saul himself recognize David's voice and the conversation becomes direct, king to fugitive, verses 17 to 20, and the chapter ends with Saul, not David, speaking last, pronouncing a blessing, verse 25. The scene keeps pulling back to a wider and more public frame, until what began as a private moral test between two men in the dark becomes a public verdict, spoken in daylight, over the whole future of the kingdom.
context.historical:
The Ziphites betraying David here is their second recorded act of the same kind, 1 Samuel 23:19 to 24 already shows them offering Saul the same information, so this chapter opens with a bitter, specific detail: these are men of Judah, David's own tribe, informing on him yet again to a Benjamite king. The wilderness of Ziph lay in the rugged hill country south of Hebron, terrain of caves and ravines that had already sheltered David more than once, and the hill of Hachilah, opposite Jeshimon, verse 3, is the same location named in the earlier betrayal, suggesting David kept returning to country he knew even though it had already cost him safety before.

Saul's camp, with the king and his general Abner lying inside the inner circle, verses 5 and 7, and troops arranged around them, reflects a standard ancient Near Eastern arrangement for a field army, valuable men protected at the center by a ring of soldiers, the same basic logic behind a defensive laager. That two men could walk to its very center and leave again undetected would have struck any ancient reader as remarkable, which is exactly why the narrator insists it was no lapse of Abner's watch but a deep sleep from the LORD, verse 12, the same kind of sleep God places on Adam in Genesis 2:21 and on Abram before the covenant promise of Genesis 15:12, a sleep that belongs to moments when God is doing something a human witness must not be awake to interrupt.
context.canonical:
By the time this chapter closes, David has now refused to kill Saul on two separate, deliberate occasions across two chapters, once by cutting only a robe, once here by taking only a spear and jug. The repetition is not narrative laziness; it is the book's way of making a conviction undeniable, so that when David is finally crowned in 2 Samuel 2 and 5, no reader can suspect his hands are stained with the blood of his predecessor.

This settled refusal becomes a template the rest of Scripture reaches for whenever it wants to describe righteous suffering under unjust power. David's own later psalms return to this posture repeatedly, I am in favor of peace, but when I speak, they want war, Psalm 120:7, and the language of entrusting one's cause to God rather than to the sword becomes almost a genre of its own in the Psalter. The New Testament picks up the same pattern explicitly when it describes Jesus before Pilate and the cross, and Peter draws directly on this kind of restraint, describing Christ who, when He suffered, made no threats but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23, language that could almost serve as commentary on David refusing Abishai's spear.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
By staging this as a second complete test rather than letting the first refusal in chapter 24 stand alone, the author forecloses an easy explanation his first readers might have reached for, that David spared Saul once because the moment caught him unprepared or overwhelmed with sudden guilt. Here David plans the whole approach in advance, walks in deliberately, and still will not lift his hand. The repetition is the argument: this is settled conviction, not a single lucky impulse of conscience.

The author also wants readers to notice who does the convicting. Saul's own words indict him more thoroughly than anything David says, I have sinned, I have played the fool, verse 21, an admission he had made almost verbatim two chapters earlier and would abandon again almost as quickly. By letting Saul confess in his own voice, twice, and letting the reader watch that confession fail to change anything lasting, the narrator prepares Israel to see David's kingship as something God secures over time, through repeated testing, rather than something Saul's changing moods could ever have granted or withheld.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what one particular fugitive did toward one particular anointed king who was actively trying to kill him; it does not lay down a universal rule that the wronged may never protect themselves or seek justice through legitimate means. David still keeps spies out, verse 4, still commands four hundred men elsewhere in this story, and still eventually accepts Saul's throne once God gives it to him, so this is not a portrait of total non resistance in every circumstance.

What does transfer as abiding instruction is the specific refusal to treat someone under God's own appointment, or more broadly anyone whose judgment belongs to God rather than to us, as fair game simply because the opportunity for revenge presents itself. David also refuses to trust his own safety to Saul's emotional confession, verse 25, going back to his own camp rather than Saul's court, a wise pattern of receiving an apology without pretending it has already produced lasting change.

debates.question: Why did David take the spear and water jug instead of simply leaving quietly?

views.label: Public proof of restraint
views.case: Taking these items let David prove beyond doubt, at a safe distance the next morning, that he had been near enough to kill Saul but chose not to, silencing any future accusation of disloyalty or rebellion.

views.label: Evidence that also indicted the guard
views.case: The missing royal spear and water jug proved not only David's restraint but Abner's failure to protect the king, turning the evidence into both a defense of David and a public rebuke of Saul's men, verses 15 to 16.

debates.bearing: Either way, David sought public vindication through visible proof rather than through violence, showing that being right before God does not require winning the argument by force.

debates.question: Does Saul's confession in verse 21 show genuine repentance?

views.label: A real if unstable softening
views.case: Saul's words echo his sorrow in chapter 24, and he goes further here, blessing David and predicting his future greatness, suggesting a moment of true, if fragile, conviction.

views.label: A repeated but hollow pattern
views.case: Saul had said nearly the same words once before, chapter 24, and would resume hunting David soon after; the repetition suggests emotional remorse without lasting change, since he offers David no restored place at court or lasting safety.

debates.bearing: David does not stake his safety on Saul's confession either way; he returns to his own men rather than to Saul's court, a wisdom that discerns between a felt emotion of sorrow and a proven change of behavior.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond the three words the basic note already names, hand, anointed, and righteousness, four more details repay a closer look.

The deep sleep that falls over Saul's whole camp, verse 12, is tardemah, the same rare word used for the sleep God places on Adam before opening his side, Genesis 2:21, and on Abram just before the covenant promise of Genesis 15:12 to 16. In each case the word marks not ordinary tiredness but a divinely imposed unconsciousness that lets God act on or around a person without their awareness, which is exactly the function it serves here: an entire armed camp cannot be walked through and out of by two men unless the LORD Himself closes every eye.

David's careful hedge in verse 19, if the LORD has stirred you up against me, uses a Hebrew verb for inciting or provoking that Scripture is willing to place in surprising company elsewhere, in the puzzling pair of verses where 2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD stirred up David against Israel to take a census, while the parallel account in 1 Chronicles 21:1 says Satan incited him to the same act. Whatever the precise relationship between those two tellings, David's own words here already show him comfortable holding two things at once, that God can stand behind a hostile human urge without becoming its author, using even an enemy's provocation to serve purposes only He fully sees.

His closing image, verse 20, like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains, names the qore, a game bird prized for being chased relentlessly across rough ground yet almost impossible to actually catch, the same bird Jeremiah later uses for someone who gathers riches unjustly, like a partridge hatching eggs it did not lay, Jeremiah 17:11. David pictures himself as prey not worth the hunt, spending Saul's army's strength for nothing.

Finally, when Saul confesses, I have played the fool, verse 21, the verb is sakal, not the nabal behind Nabal's own name one chapter earlier. Hebrew keeps a small family of words for folly, and Saul uses the same root Samuel once used of him, you have acted foolishly, 1 Samuel 13:13, after an earlier failure of nerve. Two kings' worth of folly, Nabal's contemptuous nabal and Saul's confessed sakal, frame David's story on either side, each contrasting his own repeated restraint.

typology.type: David given total power over Saul a second time, and refusing to use it, verses 8 to 12
typology.fulfillment: Abishai treats Saul's helplessness as a gift already handed over, today God has delivered your enemy into your hand, verse 8, exactly the kind of providential opening the tempter always offers alongside a shortcut to a promised reward. Jesus faces the same shape of temptation in the wilderness, offered every kingdom of the world without the cross, Matthew 4:8 to 10, and refuses it as David refuses Abishai, insisting that what the Father has promised must come by the Father's own path, not by any offered shortcut, however providential it appears.

typology.type: The spear and water jug taken as silent, undeniable proof, verses 12 and 16
typology.fulfillment: David carries away physical evidence of a mercy no one saw happen, and displays it later at a safe distance to settle, beyond dispute, both his innocence and his restraint. The risen Christ does something distantly similar, showing Thomas His pierced hands and side, John 20:27, physical proof offered after the fact of an encounter with death that ended, unlike Saul's story, not in defeat but in the plunder of death itself. David's proof only established what he had refrained from doing; Christ's wounds establish what He has already accomplished and cannot be undone.

typology.type: David, already anointed yet still hunted and uncrowned, verses 21 to 25
typology.fulfillment: Samuel anointed David chapters earlier, yet years of exile and danger still stand between that anointing and his actual reign, a gap the text never resolves quickly or tidily. Christ has likewise already been declared King through His resurrection and given all authority, yet at present we do not see everything subject to him, Hebrews 2:8, His reign is real now though not everywhere visibly acknowledged. David waited in weakness for God's timing to close the gap between anointing and throne; Christ waits in power, delaying only because the Father is patient, wanting none to perish, 2 Peter 3:9.

study.christ:
Twice already Saul has been utterly at David's mercy, and both times the temptation offered has had the same shape: a legitimate looking shortcut to a promise God has already made. Abishai does not tempt David to abandon the promise of the throne, he offers to fulfill it faster, today God has delivered your enemy into your hand, verse 8, dressing impatience up as providence. This is exactly the temptation Jesus meets in the wilderness, offered all the kingdoms of the world if only He will bow to receive them by a route that skips the cross, Matthew 4:8 to 10. Both David and Jesus recognize the same lie inside an offer that sounds like help: that God's timing needs correcting by human initiative, however righteous the initiative feels in the moment.

Saul's confession here, I have sinned, come back, David my son, verse 21, is his second such admission in as many chapters, and it changes nothing lasting; he will resume hunting David again soon after this scene ends. Against that hollow repentance the New Testament sets a King who does not merely feel sorrow and move on but who actually deals with sin, once, completely, so that by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified, Hebrews 10:14, allowing real, lasting change rather than a repeated cycle of confession and relapse. Where Saul's words could not secure David's safety even for a season, Christ's one sacrifice secures His people forever.

There is also a quieter contrast worth drawing out. David takes physical objects, a spear and a jug, as proof that he could have killed and did not, holding them up later at a safe distance to settle any dispute about his character, verses 16 and 22. The risen Christ offers something structurally similar and immeasurably greater, inviting Thomas to touch His own wounded hands and side, John 20:27, proof not of restraint from violence but of victory over the violence already done to Him. David's evidence proves an absence, a killing that did not happen. Christ's proof is of a presence, a death that did happen and has been undone.

Finally, this whole scene sits inside the same already and not yet tension that marks Christ's present reign. David has been anointed but is nowhere near his throne; Christ has been raised, exalted, and given all authority, yet Scripture is equally honest that at present we do not see everything subject to him, Hebrews 2:8. David's waiting teaches patience toward a promise not yet visible; Christ's present hidden reign asks exactly the same patience of everyone who trusts Him, right up until the day every knee will actually bow.
study.god:
God is never quoted directly in this chapter, yet the entire scene depends on things only He does. He is the reason the whole camp sleeps through an armed incursion to its very center, verse 12; He is the one whose choice between Saul's two possible ends, a natural death or death in battle, David refuses to guess at or hurry along, verse 10, leaving God more room to act than David is willing to claim for himself. A God this active behind the scenes, and this silent in the foreground, is teaching Israel that His providence does not require commentary to be real.

He is also the God who judges by information no bystander has. Long before this scene, Samuel had already been told, man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart, 1 Samuel 16:7, and this chapter plays that principle out at scale: Abishai sees only an opportunity, Abner sees only a duty he failed, and Saul, for one honest moment, sees his own guilt, but only the LORD's verdict, spoken once through Samuel back in chapter 15 and never revoked, actually decides what happens to the kingdom. David's refusal to act is itself an act of trust that God's information about Saul, and about David, is simply better than anyone else's.

This is also a God whose settled decrees outlast human emotion. Saul's confession is not necessarily insincere in the moment, I have sinned, I have played the fool, verse 21, yet it changes nothing about the sentence already passed in chapter 15, that the kingdom has been torn from him and will not return. God does not treat every fresh wave of remorse as grounds for reopening a case He has already justly closed; some doors, once shut by persistent, patterned rebellion, stay shut regardless of how the guilty party feels afterward.

Finally, God is shown here to work through very ordinary means, informants, spies, sleep, geography, without ever needing to override anyone's will to do it. No one in this chapter does anything out of character. The Ziphites betray because that is who they are, Abishai offers violence because that is his temperament, Saul confesses because for a moment his fear outweighs his pride. God's providence runs through all of it, using real human choices to arrive exactly where His own word, spoken long before any of these people acted, already said it would.

crossReferences.note: The first of David's two refusals to kill Saul, cutting only the corner of his robe in the cave at En-gedi and being stricken with conscience even for that much. Reading the two chapters side by side shows the same conviction tested under different circumstances, chance encounter there, deliberate approach here, arriving at exactly the same resolve both times.

The devil offers Jesus all the kingdoms of the world without the road of suffering that actually leads there, precisely the kind of providential shortcut Abishai offers David in this chapter. Both refusals rest on the same conviction, that what the Father has promised must come by the Father's own path, not by any offered detour.

Christ suffered unjustly and did not retaliate but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly, the New Testament's own commentary on exactly the kind of restraint David shows toward Saul, choosing to leave vindication with God rather than seizing it by his own hand.

Never take revenge, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath. Paul turns the conviction David lives out twice over into an explicit command for every believer facing injustice, do not repay evil for evil but trust a more competent judge to settle every account.

Christ did not consider equality with God something to be grasped but emptied Himself, and was afterward exalted to the highest place. The pattern of refusing to seize a rightful position by force, and receiving it instead from the Father in His own time, runs through both David's story and Christ's, though only Christ's climbs all the way to a name above every name.

Man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart. This is the very principle David trusts when he refuses to judge Saul's fate by what looks, to Abishai, like an obvious opportunity, leaving the verdict instead to the God who already knows both men completely.

The LORD stirred up David against Israel to take a census, using a verb close to the one David himself uses of a possible divine incitement against him, verse 19. Scripture is not afraid to say that God can stand behind even a hostile human urge for His own larger purposes without becoming its author.

Like a partridge hatching eggs it did not lay is one who gathers riches unjustly. Jeremiah reaches for the same game bird David names in his taunt to Saul, verse 20, each writer picturing something chased or gathered without any real, lasting claim to what is caught.

At present we do not see everything subject to him, describing Christ's present reign as real yet not everywhere visibly acknowledged. David's own position here, truly anointed yet still hunted through the wilderness, pictures in miniature this larger pattern of a genuine kingship still awaiting its full and visible display.

The risen Christ invites Thomas to touch His pierced hands and side, offering physical proof after the fact, much as David later holds up the spear and water jug as proof of a mercy no one had witnessed. Christ's wounds, unlike David's evidence, prove not restraint but a conquered death.

study.oneStory:
David's fugitive years are not one long uniform trial; they are a series of specific, escalating tests of the same conviction, and this chapter is the last and most deliberate of them before David's resolve finally cracks in the very next chapter. Twice now he has proven, once by accident and once by design, that he will not seize his own coronation by violence. That double proof matters enormously for what follows: when the crown finally does come to him, first over Judah and then over all Israel, no rival house, no lingering supporter of Saul's family, will ever be able to say with any evidence that David murdered his way to it.

Yet the very next chapter shows how costly this kind of patient waiting actually is. Chapter 27 opens with David reasoning that he will eventually be swept away by Saul's hand after all, and fleeing to the Philistines instead of trusting the LORD's timing one more time. The settled conviction on display here, refusing to force God's promise, is real, but it does not make David immune to exhaustion, and Scripture is honest enough to show both, the strength of his restraint and the fragility of the faith that produced it, sitting side by side in consecutive chapters.

This is also one more scene in the Bible's long argument that the throne of the true King is never won by seizing it. Genesis already showed Jacob refusing to force Esau's blessing back by violence, Exodus showed Moses learning the hard way that killing an Egyptian outright was not how deliverance would come, and this whole thread runs forward to its only sufficient answer, Christ, who alone could have called down legions to secure His kingdom immediately and did not, receiving instead, through suffering, a throne no betrayal, no army, and no length of exile could ever again take from Him.

quiz.q: When David found Saul asleep in the camp a second time, what did he do?

options.text: He refused to let Abishai kill Saul, insisting no one may harm the LORD's anointed, and instead took the spear and water jug as proof.
options.note: Verses 9-12 give David's explicit reasoning and his chosen action.

options.text: He took the spear and water jug from beside Saul's head and quietly left the camp.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but it omits David's stated theological reason for sparing Saul.

options.text: He debated killing Saul and let Abishai make the final call.
options.note: The opposite is true; David commanded Abishai not to touch Saul, the decision was David's alone.

options.text: He killed Saul immediately with Abishai's spear.
options.note: David explicitly forbade this and refused to strike Saul at all.

quiz.q: Why does David refuse to kill Saul, in his own stated words?

options.text: Because Saul is the LORD's anointed, and it is God alone who must remove him, whether by death, battle, or His own timing.
options.note: Verses 9-11 give this as David's reason, twice repeated.

options.text: Because killing a reigning king would break Israelite law.
options.note: David never appeals to a legal statute; his stated reason is Saul's anointed office, not a point of law.

options.text: Because Abishai talked him out of striking.
options.note: The reverse is true; Abishai urged the killing and David refused him.

options.text: Because he feared Saul's army would retaliate if he was caught.
options.note: The text gives no such fear; David and Abishai left completely undetected.

quiz.q: What proof did David use to confront Abner about failing to protect Saul?

options.text: The king's spear and water jug, taken from right beside Saul's sleeping head.
options.note: Verse 16 has David point to these missing items as evidence Abner failed his duty.

options.text: A report from spies that Saul's guard had grown careless.
options.note: David did send spies earlier, verse 4, but the direct proof shown to Abner was the physical spear and jug.

options.text: David's own unsupported testimony, without any physical evidence.
options.note: David had visible, physical proof in hand, not merely his word.

options.text: The corner of Saul's robe cut off earlier.
options.note: That was the proof used in chapter 24, at En-gedi, not in this later episode.

quiz.q: How does Saul respond when he recognizes David's voice and sees the evidence?

options.text: He confesses that he has sinned and played the fool, and he blesses David, predicting he will prevail.
options.note: Verses 21 and 25 record Saul's confession and his blessing over David.

options.text: He apologizes but insists he has done nothing wrong.
options.note: Saul explicitly says, 'I have sinned,' which is more than a bare apology without admission.

options.text: He orders his men to seize David at once.
options.note: Saul does the opposite, calling David 'my son' and promising never to harm him again.

options.text: He denies that the voice calling to him is David's at all.
options.note: Saul immediately recognizes and names David's voice, verse 17.

quiz.q: What does David ask the LORD to do in verse 23?

options.text: To repay every man for his righteousness and faithfulness, since David would not harm the LORD's anointed though he had the chance.
options.note: Verse 23 records this exact request, resting David's reward on God's just character.

options.text: To grant David the throne immediately, that same day.
options.note: David does trust God for his future, but his stated request here is about righteous reward, not an immediate crowning.

options.text: To punish Saul at once for hunting him.
options.note: David explicitly leaves Saul's fate to God's timing in verse 10, not to instant punishment here.

options.text: To make Saul forget the whole episode had happened.
options.note: David wants the episode remembered as proof of his innocence, not forgotten.

quiz.q: How does David's restraint in this chapter point toward Christ?

options.text: Like David refusing to seize the throne by violence, Jesus refused to grasp His kingdom by force, trusting the Father's justice and timing instead.
options.note: Matthew 26:52-53 and Philippians 2:6-11 draw exactly this connection.

options.text: It shows only that violence is generally an unwise strategy.
options.note: There is a true principle here, but it understates the specific theological point about God's anointed and God's timing.

options.text: It has no real connection to Christ, being only political strategy on David's part.
options.note: Scripture itself draws this connection through the pattern of the anointed one and the theme of entrusting oneself to God's justice.

options.text: It shows David lacked the courage that Christ later displayed.
options.note: The text presents David's restraint as deliberate conviction and courage, not cowardice.

questions: David again had Saul's life in his hands but chose to leave vindication to God. Where are you tempted to 'help God along' by taking justice into your own hands rather than trusting His timing?
David calls Saul 'the LORD's anointed' even while fleeing his violence. How does honoring the office or position someone holds change the way you deal with people who wrong you?
Saul confesses his sin, yet the pattern of hostility repeats, and David still keeps his distance. How do you discern between someone's genuine sorrow and a proven change in behavior?
David asks the LORD, not Saul, to repay his righteousness. Where do you look for validation or reward instead of resting in God's approval?

Jesus refused to seize His kingdom by force, entrusting Himself to the Father's justice. What would it look like for you to release a difficult situation into God's hands this week rather than forcing an outcome?

translationNotes.note: The LORD's anointed renders mashiach, the same word later used of the Messiah; here it names Saul's God-given office rather than his personal character, which is why David honors it even while fleeing Saul's violence.

Either his day will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and perish leaves the manner and timing of Saul's end entirely open, an intentional refusal by David to specify how or when, since that belongs to God alone.

If the LORD has stirred you up... may He accept an offering, but if men have done it, may they be cursed reflects an ancient assumption that unexplained royal hostility might have a hidden divine cause, while still holding any human instigators fully responsible for their part.
